title: Find the length of a linked list (traverse and count nodes).
shortTitle: Find the length of a linked list

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the length of a linked list means counting how many nodes it contains. You traverse from the head, incrementing a counter for each node, and stop when you reach null. It is O(n) time and O(1) space. Alternatively you can maintain a size field that you update on every add and remove, giving O(1) length lookups.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to know how many pending transactions Rajesh currently has in his chain. A clerk starts at the first slip and counts one, follows the arrow and counts two, and keeps going until a slip's arrow points to nothing. The final count is the number of pending transactions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk from head to null with a counter, adding one per node; or keep a size field updated as you go for instant lookups.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the length of a linked list means counting how many nodes it contains. You traverse from the head, incrementing a counter for each node, and stop when you reach null. It is O(n) time and O(1) space. Alternatively you can maintain a size field that you update on every add and remove, giving O(1) length lookups.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants to know how many pending transactions Rajesh currently has in his chain. A clerk starts at the first slip and counts one, follows the arrow and counts two, and keeps going until a slip's arrow points to nothing. The final count is the number of pending transactions.

**One line to remember:** Walk from head to null with a counter, adding one per node; or keep a size field updated as you go for instant lookups.

sections.s2_technical:
The traversal count is the direct approach. You set a counter to zero and a `current` pointer to the head. While `current` is not null, you increment the counter and advance `current` to its next. When `current` becomes null, the counter equals the number of nodes. This is O(n) because you visit every node, and O(1) space because you use one counter and one pointer.

The maintained-size approach trades a little bookkeeping for speed. You store a `size` field in the list object, increment it whenever you add a node and decrement it whenever you remove one. Then length is just returning the field, which is O(1). This is how `java.util.LinkedList` reports its size instantly rather than walking the chain each time. The cost is that every mutation must remember to update the field, so the logic is slightly more error-prone.

Which to choose depends on how often you ask for the length versus how often you mutate. If length is rarely needed, the O(n) walk is fine and avoids bookkeeping bugs. If length is read constantly, maintaining a size field is worth it. A senior nuance is consistency: if you maintain size, every single mutation path must update it, or the count drifts out of sync with reality, which is a nasty bug in a financial ledger.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India shows Rajesh a badge with the number of pending transactions in his chain. The system must count the nodes. This is exactly how finding the length works — traverse and count.

Problem 2 — The badge is refreshed on every screen, so reading the count must be cheap. This is exactly why we also maintain a size field updated on each append, giving an instant O(1) count alongside the O(n) traversal count for verification.

The code has a `TransactionNode` and a `PendingChain` class offering both `lengthByTraversal` (O(n)) and `size` (O(1) maintained). The demo builds a chain and reports both.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four appends building a chain 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000.

Step 1 — Each append links a node at the tail and increments size, so after four appends size is 4.

Step 2 — lengthByTraversal sets count to 0 and current to head. It counts the 1000 node (1), advances; counts 2000 (2); counts 3000 (3); counts 4000 (4); advances to null and stops. It returns 4.

Step 3 — size returns the maintained field 4 immediately without walking.

Step 4 — Both methods agree on 4, confirming the maintained count stayed in sync with the real structure.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Length by traversal (O(n)): 4
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Length by size field (O(1)): 4
```

```text
    │
    └─ size(): return maintained field → 4             (O(1))
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the length of a linked list means counting its nodes, and there are two approaches. The direct approach is to traverse: I set a counter to zero and a current pointer to the head, then I walk the chain, incrementing the counter for each node and advancing until I reach null. That is linear time and constant space. The faster approach is to maintain a size field on the list that I increment on every add and decrement on every remove, so asking for the length is just returning that field in constant time, which is exactly how Java's own LinkedList reports its size instantly.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I show Rajesh a badge with the number of pending transactions in his chain. Because that badge is refreshed every time the screen loads, I maintain a size field so reading the count is a constant-time operation rather than walking the whole chain on every refresh.

The nuance I always raise is consistency. If I maintain a size field, then every single code path that adds or removes a node must update that field, otherwise the count silently drifts out of sync with the real structure. In a financial ledger that kind of drift is a serious bug, so I keep a traversal-based count available too, which I can use in tests or audits to verify that the maintained size still matches the actual number of nodes. The choice between the two comes down to how often I read the length versus how often I mutate the list.
